author: aleabitoreddit
text:
Just from my personal experiences:

My new heuristic is markets tend to price things in ~8 months in advance unless your theme is Space, Robotics/Quantum.

For themes I'm tracking:

For photonics:
- Next-gen pluggables (1.6T) are right around now (ex. $LITE, $COHR, Innolight, etc.) then $AAOI, $JBL 1.6T LRO and other later bloomers H1 2027.
- CPO Scale Out related stuff is late H2 2026 (ex. $POET, Shunsin, etc)
- NPO stuff H2 2026/2027 prob as bridge architectures
- CPO Scale Up H2 2027 (ex. Ayar, Celestial, etc).

If I use the 8 month rule like 4 months too early for CPO Scale Up Names.

But in hindsight, I wanted to be early this time around given I felt this was the most compelling architectural shift given GS tam projections + markets seem to disagree, which is why there's a selloff with Foci/MSScorp and others.

Maybe it should start picking up again and start to be priced in December 2026 IG? idk we'll see.

Stuff like lasers, $AXTI (InP substrates) are used across all those themes. FAU/silicon photonics/PCB midplanes, etc. are more concentrated around different architectures.

Memory theme is quite a massive bottleneck as you've been seeing:
- HBM3e around now as you've seen with Micron, Samsung, Sk Hynix etc. and NAND with Sandisk.
- HBM4 mass production right around now too with SK Hynix, Micron/Samsung.
- HBF 2027?

But again these are the same Kioxia, Samsung, Sk Hynix, $MU, Kioxia players across different architectures, and we're seeing re-rating cause we're mid-bottleneck. So these are likely to keep compounding.

Glass Substrates:
H2 2026 start with SKC Absolics (probably just early stage ramp). H2 2027-2028 is where the fun begins, with 2028 TSM CoPoS, others like Samsung etc. 2027, and Intel later on.

Humanoid Suppliers:
Very early, but as I said with Space markets probably won't wait to price this in with Elon giving bullish $TSLA optimus projections and Chinese humanoid companies like Unitree/AGI Bot starting to ramp up.

Neoclouds:
I said this was probably the buildout period for many of the players and Q4 2026 earnings is when some of the leaders typically hit inflection. Maybe was a bit early focusing so hard H4 2025 last year. Like with $NBIS $7-9B ARR, that ARR proj should hit Q4 earnings. If we apply that ~8M rule, Jan/Feb was very depressing, but should have bought in March 2026 rather than Sept last year. But markets might be pricing in Feb 2027 window.

So I'm personally probably going to repositioning right now around: Memory, Neoclouds, Photonics, Robotics. Probably heavier when something is ~8m in advance or captures many different themes eg. $SIVE for pluggable, NPO, CPO, and all architectures. And just having exposure to mini-shifts in between like advanced packaging materials, hybrid bonding for memory, or random bottlenecks like MLCCs.

I probably shouldn't have heavy exposure to something way out 12M+ if I rethink my decisions. Also something to note is machine suppliers in general hit revenue faster than the general volume ramp, with your main companies like Samsung, Absolics, etc. need machines to get going in the first place. Which is why I ended up getting $LPK positions personally.

I should follow my personal 8 rule to the T myself since I probably was a little too early to many names. Those are just my own experiences tho I'm learning along the way.

author: aleabitoreddit
text:
Samsung/SK Hynix Supplier Korean Stock Idea:

It's kinda like $SIVE + CPO mixed with 
$AEHR
 but for memory (and less TAM).

Auros (322310): ~$210m MC.

It's the SK Hynix and Samsung supplier for next-gen HBM.

This is a direct play for HBM4e hybrid bonding (every memory maker) + HBM4 (samsung) / metrology.

A comparison is $SIVE for CPO, where they weren't really around for  HBM3 (photonics equivalent is like 800g) and have been developing the  past many years. But with next-gen it's there for volume ramp.

It's the only Korean Domestic company for IR metrology. And product #1 is used for hybrid bonding.

So Samsung HBM4 lines use hybrid copper bonding in 2026, so they're trying to push overlay tool through qualification H2?

Sk Hynix actually just used MR-MUF (no hybrid bonding) for HBM4. But  Trendforce reported today SK Hynix has completed 12-high hybrid  bonding HBM validation and is raising yields for mass production?

So maybe SK Hynix are adopters too soon, which is bullish. 

But at least for short-term it's probably Samsung first for volume if qualifications pass.

$KLA is a pure monopoly over this sort of IR metrology overlay that Korea (SK Hynix/Samsung) wants to break.

So Samsung they are likely using Auros to customize IR tools and keep domestic secrets.

Think of it as the Korean 
$INTC
 where they will use their domestic  champion as much as possible if it actually works. And both will ramp up  HBM4E -> HBM5 with this technology, so multiple years capex.

For product #2 (this is why I mention 
$AEHR
, similar):

There's also the "AUROS Technology Inc. is conducting qualification  testing of its ultra-precision thin-film thickness measurement equipment  with a major  domestic chipmaker".

This was dominated by $KLA and 
$AMAT
 before.

"Development began at its research center, followed by pilot   manufacturing at a new facility from 2021, with about four years  required to reach the current qualification stage"

Basically they've been developing many years + qualifying now, and  around h2 if it passes it switches to high volume production for 2027.

So this is the sweet spot for timelines. It's really high risktho ...

But high reward, lower downside risk given Samsung/SK Hynix are kinda supporting this company. (disclosure: have positions, NFA, DYOR)

Anyway, still doing reserach into this but found it compelling, just my thoughts so far.

TLDR:

Not really well known $210M MC supplier to Samsung/SK Hynix.

Then both of their main product lines finish qualification h2 for  volume ramp 2027? So h1 into h2 (now) seemed like the sweet spot.

Still doing research of course, new company to me. just caught my eye. Very very early of course before any movement.

Disclosure:  These are high confidence links to Sivers, customers are likely to  remain unconfirmed as the supply chain BOM/customer relationships are  heavily guarded and under NDA. It’s also possible some of these high  confidence relationships may not proceed to mass production. 
___

Sivers also announced in their 2025 annual report:

1. “We are currently seeing great interest... testing our DFB lasers across multiple manufacturers in pluggable transceivers”

"Our  serviceable markets have now been expanded to include pluggable optical  interconnects as well as scale-up and scale-out architectures for  co-packaged" (TAM expansion)

There are likely more  hyperscaler suppliers not listed here yet that Sivers is  sampling/qualifying with on the pluggable transceiver side. 

2. "Discussions with hyperscalers and pluggable transceiver suppliers indicate a shortage of CW lasers in the coming years"

LITE in their recent 2026 earnings transcript announced they faced a CW laser bottlenecks. 

As a result, Lumentum they had to buy externally from competitors (likely Sumitomo/Furukawa). 

Sivers likely has capacity locked in with Win from this nuance. 

“The  partnership announced with high-volume supplier Win Semiconductor in  March 2025 now gives us a strong position to meet growing demand” 

And many of the other CPO programs outside of Broadcom / Nvidia, such as AMD likely went to Sivers and other suppliers. 

___

For the overall optical TAM, per Goldman Sachs research report:
“We  expect the aggregate dollar content per computing unit across scale up  and scale out to increase by 29x from US$315k in GB300 NVL72 to US$9.4bn  in Rubin Ultra NVL576, and assuming the numbers of racks through the  full product cycle are 48k racks for GB300 NVL72, and 16.5k computing  units for Rubin Ultra NVL576, the aggregate value TAM across scale up  and scale out would increase by 9x from US$15bn in GB300 NVL72 (mainly  in 2026) to US$154bn in Rubin Ultra NVL576 (mainly in 2028). 

Among the US$154bn value TAM, 69% goes to scale up, or US$106bn, and CPO contributes US$91bn, or 59% of the US$154bn value TAM, assuming CPO at 29% penetration rate in scale out.”

author: aleabitoreddit
text:
Hard to see a world where US AI hyperscaler capex drops dramatically from 
$GOOGL
 to 
$META
.

When China entities like 360 go and claim:

They now have a "AI cyber nuclear weapon" that can hack Western companies and governments.

(Zhou claimed Mythos was like an AI era cyber nuclear weapon, then claimed they built a Chinese equivalent).

We're probably witnessing the modern cold war.

But instead of nuclear stockpiles, it's racing to build superintelligence both offensively and defensively.

With many different "battles" happening concurrently like supply chain export controls between China -> Japan -> US hyperscalers.

The funny thing is that everyone still depends on one another:

- US with things like rare earths and feedstock from China.
- China with EUV to EDA and engineered substrates.

So there's still give or takes trades to build up capabilities like Nvidia/AMD AI chips access for rare-earth/magnets access.

Which is exactly why it's important for the US to build up rare earths supply chains ASAP.

And not piss off allied supply chain chokepoints like European EUV partners with 
$ASML
 to Japanese vacuum/furnace makers like Ulvac with things like tariffs, if the US wants to use it as leverage for negotiations.

But we're getting dangerously closer to a point where supply chain interdependence is not a deterrent against escalation.

Especially as China grows closer to becoming self-reliant. And that might be the tipping point.

views.why: hard to see hyperscaler AI capex dropping given the geopolitical AI arms-race dynamics between the US and China
same reasoning — capex unlikely to drop given the intensifying AI arms race
named only in the context of chip access being used as a rare-earth trade negotiating lever
named only as an allied supply-chain chokepoint the US should avoid alienating, a geopolitical caution rather than a stock case

author: aleabitoreddit
text:
TSM | Serenity subscriber-only: advanced packaging may ramp earlier, while the auto semiconductor chain could be nearing a bottom

In Serenity’s subscriber-only note on June 4, 2026, TSM management pointed to two signals worth paying attention to.

First, CoPoS / advanced packaging may be progressing faster than the market expects.
TSM’s chairman said CoPoS could become very large within the next 2–3 years, and that pilot lines are already running. Serenity’s interpretation is that the market has been treating this as a story for much later, but if volumes begin ramping within the next few years, related opportunities may enter the market’s focus earlier than expected. She also noted that VisEra, a TSM subsidiary with relevant exposure, has already started to show signs of re-rating.

Second, autos and robotics could be the next growth inflection point.
TSM highlighted autonomous robots and autonomous vehicles as future growth areas, and that caught Serenity’s attention. Auto semiconductors have been in a slump for the past two years, so if signals like this are starting to emerge now, the market may be underestimating the possibility of a bottoming process in the auto semiconductor chain.

She also briefly flagged XFAB.
The reason is that XFAB has meaningful exposure to the automotive segment. If autonomous driving and the broader auto supply chain do recover from this downturn, previously pressured names like XFAB could become worth revisiting.

In short, Serenity is not pointing to a short-term catalyst here, but to two earlier-stage industry signals: advanced packaging may begin scaling sooner than expected, and the auto semiconductor chain may also be approaching a bottom.

views.why: management signals suggest CoPoS/advanced packaging may progress faster than the market expects, with pilot lines already running and a subsidiary already showing signs of re-rating

its meaningful automotive exposure means a recovery in autonomous driving and the broader auto chain, which TSMC flagged as a coming growth area, could make a previously pressured name worth revisiting

text:
📌 2026-06-07, Serenity Subscriber-Only Insight: A New AI Memory Battleground Around HBF Is Heating Up, and Packaging Equipment Names May Benefit First

Serenity’s latest subscriber-only post suggests that the next wave of opportunity in the AI memory space may be expanding from HBM into HBF (High Bandwidth Flash). While it is still difficult to accurately estimate the ultimate market size of HBF, if the industry begins moving toward commercialization, the earliest beneficiaries may not be end products, but rather upstream advanced packaging equipment players.

The core logic she highlights is very clear: TC bonders (thermal compression bonding equipment) could become one of the earliest areas to see expectations start pricing in. These tools are mainly used to stack and connect memory chips under high heat and pressure. Once HBF moves closer to volume production, demand for this type of equipment could be among the first things the market begins to trade on.

The key companies Serenity mentioned include:

• Hanmi Semiconductor: Seen as the strongest first mover at the moment and what she views as the leading name
• Hanwha Semiconductor: Also considered a first mover and one of the most important equipment names to track closely
• ASMPT
• K&S

Among them, the first two look more like the core leadership names, while the latter two are more “entry” candidates that could also attract market attention if the HBF theme continues to broaden.

The key point of this subscriber-only insight is not that HBF has already fully arrived, but rather that when the market starts pre-positioning for HBF commercialization, equipment names are often the first group to move.

If you are also watching AI memory, advanced packaging, and semiconductor equipment, this is a theme worth tracking closely from here.

text:
📌 2026-06-21, Serenity Subscriber-Only Insight: Nvidia’s healthcare narrative may be spilling over, with organ-on-chip emerging as a new niche theme

In her latest subscriber-only post, Serenity said she recently started digging into the organ-on-chip space and followed a new thread from there: Darwin, a company previously associated more with display/module-related business, is now moving into biosensors, biochips, and biomedical testing. At the same time, the company is working with Anivance AI on bionic organ chips and other biomedical testing solutions.

What makes this more interesting for the market is the narrative layer around it: Anivance AI is being framed with an “Nvidia backdrop.” That opens the door for investors to read this theme as: AI + Nvidia exposure + healthcare tech + organ-on-chip.

Serenity’s real point is not that this industry has already entered a mature monetization phase. It is that this may be a very early-stage branch theme with room for narrative expansion. If Nvidia’s market narrative truly starts extending further into biomedical and healthcare applications, the first names to get attention may not be the most established leaders, but rather smaller edge names that get pulled into the concept trade first.

That said, there are clear reasons to stay cautious:

• “Nvidia backdrop” does not mean a direct Nvidia partnership
• Darwin still looks more like a cross-sector expansion story, with commercialization not yet fully proven
• If these names move in the short term, the rally may be driven by narrative and sentiment first, not fundamentals

In short, this subscriber-only post is pointing to an early signal: Nvidia’s spillover into healthcare and biotech may be helping create a new speculative niche around organ-on-chip.

Not quite sure why IBK and other institutions are a fan of linearly modeling S-curve volume ramps... 

Like adding +10K per year, don't quite think it's volume ramp is going to work like that... if I had to guess it would look more like: 

- 15-20k 2028
- 40k-70k 2029
- 90k-140k for 2030

Since Boston Dynamics is projecting 30k capacity by 2028 (I'm sure they'd aim to get more online by 2029-2030), as China collectively is already doing 100k EOY in 2026.  

In terms of competitive landscape they name:

- 
$TSLA
, Figure, Apptronik, 
$CCXI
 (Agility), as US  players. Then Boston Dynamics (Korea parent owned now)
- Unitree, Fourier, AGibot, UBtech, 
$XPEV
 as the Chinese leaders. 
- Neura, Pal Robotics, Wandercraft, Oversonic, as the EU leaders.  

They also did quite a lot of valuation modeling around Hyundai Mobis/Hyundai Autoever/Glovis. 

Regarding the BD economic ownership from 27.9% from Hyundai Motor, 11.3% from Mobis, and 11.3% from Glovis. So at least institution are valuing humanoid segments inside companies lot more now. 

Then from report assumptions:
- 31 actuators per Atlas
- $1K per actuator in 2028
- $134K Atlas ASP,

Which implies actuator cost of final selling price is roughly 23–28%. 

Probably the more interesting statement was IBK stated that actuator capacity is biggest signal for volume ramp. eg. every 310,000 units of actuator capacity supports 10,000 more robots. 

So tracking actuator outputs, yields, ASP is a cleaner read on 2028-2030 ramp.

I didn't have much personal takeaways, but hopefully others find it interesting, maybe around Hwashin as a core supplier or around actuator capacity as an indicator.

text:
Lot of people were curious about $SIVE capacity volume ramp modeling through fab-light (Win Semi + others):

Using 10% of Win's wafer capacity as a low-end allocation (65% yield assumption, $50-$75 ASP):

Sivers would support $341-$512M worth of annual array revenue. Given upper end of managements 50-60%+ gross margin target, would be roughly:

$205–307M of annual gross profit.

Against Sivers current ~$1.1B MC, would be ~:

3.6–5.4× MC/gross profit if this capacity scenario plays out in 2028.  

And at 15% would be $307–461M in gross profit (2.4–3.6× MC/gross profit)

Sivers CEO also replied that they're working with more fabs for capacity. And from an older deck, there looks to be more qualifications since 2024.  

So capacity targets might be larger than what's stated here as CPO takes off. 

I also expect to see revenue pipeline projections hiked in future quarters, as more qualification suppliers to into HVM. 
_

As for demand side, CW also happens to be very bottlenecked. 

Lumentum are buying CW off the open market due to EML obligations from their ER transcript. 

And 
$AMD
 are signing LTAs to secure CW capacity (from Trendforce). So when Sivers is ramping with 
$GFS
, 
$JBL
, Ayar, 
$POET
, O-NET and others... 

Given the current constraints, it's highly likely any  independent qualified capacity that comes online would be absorbed.  

And as a cherry on top, Morgan Stanley named $SIVE (~$1.1B) as one of the three leading CPO laser players .

Alongside $55B+ players Coherent and Lumentum in their recent note for a reason...

_

TLDR: Sivers only needs a low end allocation from Win to make substantial gross income relative to current valuations. 

I think the largest revenue upside that isn't modeled in if they TAM expansion with M&A after US NASDAQ listing. 

By copying the Lumentum playbook with Cloud Light to build out entire transceiver modules or with optical engines.

$LITE

$SNDK

$AMKR

$GOOGL
 capex raised to $195-$205B, which is typically the biggest AI demand signal from hyperscalers.

$AAOI
.

 compute and

And my guess is that we'll see the theme recover broadly. But I can't predict what hour, day, or week that happens.

 COUPE [ likely maps to $NVDA 
 CPO products] - "The CPO piece does flow through that 10% customer"

"The rapid recent growth of our CPO business is an exciting development, which we believe represents the very early stages of widespread adoption of silicon photonics in the broader semiconductor industry"

text:
Few earnings TLDRs with my favorite $AXTI and $AMZN:

Amazon:
- Raised 2026 capex to $220B vs. prior $200B (partly due to higher memory costs, which is bullish on $MU to Samsung) 
- Even at $220B, Amazon will not have enough capacity to meet all 2026 demand; Jassy expects the same in 2027.
- Most incoming 2027 capacity is already reserved, with substantial 2028 capacity also reserved.

Mostly read through on upstream semis. $GOOGL, $META, $AMZN, and $MSFT all identified compute shortage. 

All the narratives a few weeks earlier was "excess compute" from Meta and others + hyperscalers cutting back on spend... All BS. 

Amazon earnings was very bullish on AI semi trade. 

AXTI:

- AXT to double InP capacity during 2026. Then double again in 2027. 

This is expected to make AXT "by far the largest indium phosphide producer in the world." - LFG

- Q2 rev was $47.6M, the highest quarterly revenue in AXT history (InP revenue reached a record $30.7M, from DC applications.)
- Revenue increased 77% sequentially and 164% year over year.
- InP revenue-capacity targets: $60M per quarter exiting 2026.
- $130M per quarter exiting 2027 

That $130m target could be hiked too since management stated they find "whatever ways to increase that capacity expansion"

- Management said the reported backlog remains well above $100M, but that number no longer reflects all available demand.

"Customer demand continues to outpace supply, no matter how fast we add capacity." 800G/1.6T is driving the current cycle, while NPO/CPO extends it beyond 2027. 

Also they're targeting 50%-plus gross margin: "We should definitely be targeting a number that begins with a five."

China demand more than doubled, and their agreements with Casela, $COHR and $LITE did not materially drive Q2. 

This is not even considering my projected massive ASP hikes yet as InP substrates get more bottlenecked. 

TLDR:

- Amazon too much compute demands, needs capex to fufill it, so upstream semis go brrr. 
- AXT world largest InP substrate supplier, high gross margins, expansion, and supply can't keep up with demand.  

Bullish on demand side from Amazon + capex. Bullish on upstream optical supply chains from too much demand. https://x.com/aleabitoreddit/status/2083088870942642391

text: Semiconductor expert: The only citable POET/Sivers language is 'production readiness by end of 2026', with customer prototypes in H1 2026. A readiness milestone is not a production order, and no volume, customer or ASP has been disclosed by either company.

author: fundamental
text: Fundamental analyst: Q1 2026 net sales were SEK 61.9m, down 22% year on year. The $799m headline is an opportunity pipeline, not backlog or revenue, and grew off a base the company itself does not convert. Revenue is shrinking while the story expands.

author: pm
text: Portfolio manager: Nothing financial confirms the laser ramp before the Q2 interim report on 27 August 2026. Any position added on the POET wording upgrade is being taken ahead of the only print that can test it.

author: semi-expert
text: Semiconductor expert: Confirmed on the FQ3 2026 call: supply-demand imbalance greater than 30% in EMLs and pump lasers, Japan wafer fab fully allocated, laser chip shipments double the year-ago quarter. The shortage is real and fab-limited, not order-limited.

author: fundamental
text: Fundamental analyst: FQ3 2026 revenue was a record $808m, up 90% year on year, led by transceivers and laser chips. The revenue is landing, not merely forecast.

author: pm
text: Portfolio manager: The shortage evidence is the CEO's own remarks, so citing him is not independent corroboration. Meanwhile Lumentum is committing $87m of deposits to AXT to reserve InP substrate through 2031 — the input is scarce enough to require prepayment.

author: semi-expert
text: Semiconductor expert: FQ1 2027 data center revenue was a record $75.2bn, up 92% year on year, with networking revenue near tripling. The Blackwell 300 ramp and the scale-up interconnect attach rate are both confirmed in the filing, not inferred.

author: fundamental
text: Fundamental analyst: NVIDIA returned roughly $20bn to shareholders in the quarter and authorised a further $80bn of buyback while raising the dividend 25x. That is capital returned, not capacity added — the supply constraint sits at packaging and optics, not at NVIDIA's balance sheet.

author: pm
text: Portfolio manager: At 74.9% gross margin NVIDIA is the customers' cost line. Meta missed Q2 EPS at $6.18 against a $7.14 consensus while raising capex. The first evidence of buyer P&L strain shows up in the payer's earnings, not in NVIDIA's.

author: semi-expert
text: Semiconductor expert: The 800G ramp is company-confirmed: Q2 shipments guided at nearly four times Q1 levels off a record $151.1m Q1. The volume inflection is real even where the CPO customer identity is not disclosed.

author: fundamental
text: Fundamental analyst: The company guides Q2 2026 revenue to $180-198m and FY2026 to roughly $1.1bn. A $471m monthly rate, or $5.6bn annualised in 2027, is about five times the run-rate management itself has guided to. That gap is the whole bull case.

author: pm
text: Portfolio manager: Q2 is guided to non-GAAP EPS between -$0.03 and +$0.03 on 29-30% gross margin. At record revenue the company is at breakeven, so a one-times-forward-revenue multiple is cheap only against a top line that earns nothing.

author: semi-expert
text: Semiconductor expert: 2026 capex guidance of $130-145bn includes finance lease principal, and the low end rose $10bn in one quarter. Part of that increase is memory cost inflation rather than incremental compute units, so capex dollars overstate unit demand growth for suppliers.

author: fundamental
text: Fundamental analyst: Q2 2026 EPS was $6.18 against roughly $7.14 expected, on $60.8bn revenue and $31.1bn of quarterly capex. The desk's recap carried the capex number and not the earnings miss or the free cash flow compression underneath it.

author: pm
text: Portfolio manager: Shares fell roughly 8% on the print. The supplier read-through stays intact while the payer is derated, so owning Meta and owning its suppliers are now opposite trades, not the same one.

author: semi-expert
text: Semiconductor expert: Roughly 60% of the raised capex goes to servers and 40% to data centers and networking equipment. Only that 40% slice reads through to the optics and interconnect names the desk owns, so headline capex overstates the addressable pull.

author: fundamental
text: Fundamental analyst: Q2 2026 revenue of $119.8bn was up 24%, with Google Cloud at $24.8bn up 82% and quarterly capex at a record $44.9bn. Full-year capex guidance was raised to $195-205bn. The spend is funded by an accelerating cloud business.

author: pm
text: Portfolio manager: The stock fell about 5% after a revenue beat, on the capex raise alone. The market is currently paying for AI demand with multiple compression at the buyer, which is the same mechanism that would eventually cap the buyer's willingness to spend.

author: semi-expert
text: Semiconductor expert: The CPO adoption claim rests on channel checks and a Rosenblatt note, not on any AMD disclosure. author: fundamental
text: Fundamental analyst: Q1 2026 data center revenue was $5.8bn, up 57% year on year, with Q2 guided to roughly $11.2bn plus or minus $300m, about 46% growth at the midpoint. The accelerator business is compounding independently of the CPO narrative.

author: pm
text: Portfolio manager: Q2 results land on 4 August, one day out. The guide already embeds 46% growth, so the print is a near-term binary on execution rather than on the AI thesis, and adding size into it is a timing decision, not a view.

author: semi-expert
text: Semiconductor expert: Nebius secured up to 1.2GW of power and land for an owned site in Pennsylvania and expects more than 3GW contracted by year-end. For a neocloud the binding constraint is energised capacity, and that constraint is being cleared ahead of the revenue.

author: fundamental
text: Fundamental analyst: Q1 2026 revenue was $399.0m, which annualises near $1.6bn against a full-year target of $3-3.4bn. Almost the entire guide sits in the second half and depends on capacity landing on schedule.

author: pm
text: Portfolio manager: Capex plans are an order of magnitude above revenue, so the equity is a financing story before it is a compute story. The risk that matters is the terms of the next raise, not the demand for GPUs.

author: semi-expert

Whether the named category captures Agility's addressable market is not established by any primary source I can cite.

author: fundamental
text: Fundamental analyst: The business combination values Agility at roughly $2.5bn with over $620m of gross proceeds. That is a valuation negotiated in a SPAC agreement against pre-scale revenue, not one set by a market, and it is the anchor for every multiple quoted since.

author: pm
text: Portfolio manager: CCXI is a pre-close SPAC. Exposure to Agility only exists after SEC review of the S-4, a shareholder vote and closing expected before end-2026, after which it trades as AGLT. Deal and redemption risk currently sit above operating risk.

author: semi-expert
text: Semiconductor expert: Only about 20% of DRAM and 30% of NAND volume is covered by the 16 strategic customer agreements. Roughly four fifths of DRAM volume remains exposed to spot pricing, so the contracts smooth the cycle rather than remove it.

author: fundamental
text: Fundamental analyst: Fiscal Q3 DRAM revenue was a record $31.3bn, up 343% year on year at 84.9% consolidated gross margin, with 16 strategic customer agreements and remaining performance obligations above $5bn. The demand lock is contractual, not anecdotal.

author: pm
text: Portfolio manager: An 84.9% gross margin is a cycle peak, not a run-rate. The agreements defend floor prices and volume, not the pricing above the floor, which is exactly the part currently carrying the earnings.

author: semi-expert
text: Semiconductor expert: 18A yields, 18A-P risk production and the 14A PDK 0.9 milestone come from call commentary I cannot tie to a primary filing. On the disclosed schedule, 14A risk production is 2027 and high-volume ramp 2028, so external foundry revenue is not a 2026 or 2027 event.

author: fundamental
text: Fundamental analyst: Q2 2026 revenue was $16.1bn, up 25% and the strongest growth in over fifteen years, yet GAAP EPS was negative $2.16 against non-GAAP $0.42. The fastest growth in a decade and a half still does not produce a GAAP profit.

author: pm
text: Portfolio manager: Q3 is guided to $15.8-16.8bn revenue and $0.38 non-GAAP EPS, above consensus. The China CPU long-term agreement story driving the desk's interest is a Reuters report, not company disclosure, and appears nowhere in the release.

author: semi-expert
text: Semiconductor expert: The agreement reserves a minimum annual indium phosphide commitment running through 31 December 2031 and supports additional capacity if required. No wafer volumes, pricing or capacity figures are disclosed, so the technical scale of the reservation cannot be sized from the filing.

author: fundamental
text: Fundamental analyst: The deal is two deposits of $43.5m, $87m in total, the second only in calendar 2028. Both operate as shipment credits offset against future invoices, not fees. The desk recorded one $43.5m payment and treats it as reservation income; it is a customer prepayment.

author: pm
text: Portfolio manager: Revenue recognition is deferred behind the credits, so the cash arrives years before the earnings do. Concentration also rises: the same handful of laser makers reserving capacity through 2031 are the only buyers of the reserved output.

author: aleabitoreddit
text:
Yes, I'm still bullish on memory like $MU / Samsung.

As I said earlier, markets tend to rotate from bottleneck to bottleneck.

This week it looks $AXTI to $LITE in the photonics sector is the focus again. 

The thing is... the primary thing that changed are the stock prices, followed by some narratives + updates sprinkled in here and there.

For photonics:

> We already knew $COHR / $LITE lasers were completely sold out for the next 2 years during July's drop. 

> We knew about demand imbalance from $AAOI from last quarter's earnings calls.

Nothing deteriorated fundamentally during July's crash, other than listed price after liquidations. 

Yet tons of people called $AAOI a "scam" when it dropped to $75, or $AXTI a "scam" on its drop to $35... 

But are bullish again at $140 or $80, when the transciver/InP substrate bottleneck hasn't changed at all, but maybe even got worse... (eg. draft for US ban on new china optical transceivers, scale up demand projections)

For Memory:

I'm witnessing a lot of retail capitulation, but the same people I'm seeing were mega bullish after $MU signed 16 SCAs and gave exceptional projections a month ago. 

Or were celebrating Samsung having the highest operating profit in the world.

There's updates here and there eg. Rubin Ultra with memory optimizations (which Nvidia strives for every generation), with prices no longer being hiked way above expectations to the extreme. 

But the operating income relative to MC is just absurd around current prices, especially memory becomes structural. 

And the demand imbalance should be even worse next year.  

People tend to capitulate and follow narratives when a sector drops (eg. Helium/LNG back in Iran war), even if the bottleneck or fundamental situation hasn't really changed much (eg. $SPCX Elon earnings call reiterating memory tightness). 

I can't tell others what to to do: 

But $AAOI at $140 and $AAOI at $75 are the same company.

Samsung at a $1.5T MC and Samsung at a $980B MC are the same company. 

Just valuations and narratives (often noise) change, and markets rotate from sector to sector. https://x.com/aleabitoreddit/status/2086148557187461412

author: semi-expert
text: Semiconductor expert: The $427m capacity model rests on a pipeline, not orders. Sivers' own Q1 2026 report describes a $799M opportunity pipeline and revenue hurt by the US shutdown. No shipped InP laser volume has been disclosed, so wafer-allocation maths cannot be checked against anything the company has reported.

author: fundamental
text: Fundamental analyst: Valuation runs ahead of any reported number: no Q2 figures exist until the 27 August 2026 interim report, so a ~SEK 13bn market cap is supported only by Q1's pipeline disclosure. Every revenue estimate in the feed is modelled, none is reported.

author: pm
text: Portfolio manager: Worst entry point of the cycle: the stock has run hard into a binary. The 27 August interim report is the first hard datapoint, and it either shows InP revenue converting or it does not. Sizing now pays full price for information that is seventeen days away.

author: semi-expert
text: Semiconductor expert: The $500M+ Q4 figure is a call remark, not guidance. AOI's release guides Q3 to $255-290M and reaffirms roughly $1.1B for the year, which implies Q4 near $500M only at the very top. Doing it needs a near-doubling on capacity the company itself calls constrained.

author: fundamental
text: Fundamental analyst: Margins went backwards while revenue grew 86%. GAAP gross margin was 27.7% versus 30.3% a year ago and 29.1% last quarter, and non-GAAP EPS was $0.06. The ramp is being bought with mix and cost, so operating leverage is not yet showing up.

author: pm
text: Portfolio manager: At roughly ten times this year's guided revenue after a violent weekly re-rate, the shortage is priced. Downside case is a mid-2027 capacity slip or the China transceiver ban being shelved. What forces an exit is gross margin failing to clear 30% next quarter.

author: semi-expert
text: Semiconductor expert: Meta's disclosure gives capex dollars and nothing else. There is no accelerator mix, no useful-life assumption and no optics content in the release, so the $130-145B cannot be converted into GPU or transceiver unit demand from the filing itself. Any such read-through is an estimate.

author: fundamental
text: Fundamental analyst: Free cash flow essentially disappeared: $784M in Q2 against $31.1B of capex, and full-year capex was narrowed upward to $130-145B. The buildout is now consuming the cash generation that made Meta a self-funding compounder, which is why the multiple is compressing.

author: pm
text: Portfolio manager: Meta is the hyperscaler where the market has already voted against capex. Owning it as an AI-demand proxy means accepting a shrinking free-cash-flow yield with no disclosed return-on-capex metric. What changes the call is capex guidance flattening rather than rising again.

author: semi-expert
text: Semiconductor expert: 'Sold out' cannot be sized from the filing. Nebius reports capacity fully contracted and capex of $20-25B, but discloses no contracted megawatts, delivery schedule or customer names. The claim is therefore unauditable in either direction until contract detail is published.

author: fundamental
text: Fundamental analyst: The equity is a levered call on execution. Q1 revenue was $399M against capex guided to $20-25B, funded by $4.3B of convertibles, an NVIDIA equity stake and secured debt at SOFR plus 250bps. Any slip in customer ramp lands on a financed balance sheet, not on cash.

author: pm
text: Portfolio manager: Q2 results land 12 August, two days away, so position size taken now is a coin-flip on disclosure. The operative question is whether prepayments are being recognised as demand. What would force an exit is capex rising again without contracted revenue rising with it.

author: semi-expert
text: Semiconductor expert: The fifth InP fab is a conversion, not new capacity. Greensboro is being converted from gallium arsenide, which needs process transfer and customer requalification measured in quarters. The 30%-plus supply gap management describes therefore does not close inside fiscal 2027 on this asset.

author: fundamental
text: Fundamental analyst: Guidance already assumes near-perfection: fiscal Q4 revenue of $960M-$1.01B at 35-36% non-GAAP operating margin and EPS of $2.85-$3.05. At the current market capitalisation that is a mid-teens multiple of annualised sales, so the shortage is capitalised, not anticipated.

author: pm
text: Portfolio manager: Results are due 11 August, one day away, after a near-50% weekly move. Buying into that is paying peak positioning for a known event. The exit trigger is an in-line print with unchanged capacity commentary, which the current price does not allow for.

author: semi-expert
text: Semiconductor expert: MI450 is a 2027 revenue event, not a 2026 one. The Q2 data-centre growth came from EPYC and MI350-series parts; Helios entered production with shipments starting only at the end of Q3, and the Anthropic deployment begins its first gigawatt in the first half of 2027.

author: fundamental
text: Fundamental analyst: Data-centre revenue was $6.7B in the quarter, up 107% year over year from $3.2B. The growth is real and filed, but it is still roughly a tenth of NVIDIA's data-centre run-rate, so AMD remains a share-gain story rather than a second incumbent.

author: pm
text: Portfolio manager: The 2027 doubling is already the consensus case, and the largest committed volumes do not ship until the first half of 2027. That leaves three quarters of proof-free carry. What would force an exit is Helios slipping past the end of Q3 shipment commitment.

author: semi-expert
text: Semiconductor expert: Coherent's own numbers confirm the datacom pull: Q3 fiscal 2026 revenue of $1.81B, up 21% year over year, with the increase attributed to the datacenter business and higher communications demand. Fiscal Q4 is guided to $1.91-$2.05B, so the ramp is disclosed, not inferred.

author: fundamental
text: Fundamental analyst: Coherent is priced like a laser pure-play but is not one. Non-GAAP gross margin was 39.6%, well below component peers, because industrial, telecom and materials segments dilute the datacenter mix. The re-rating assumes a margin structure the reported segments do not yet produce.

author: pm
text: Portfolio manager: A large part of this move discounts a proposed US ban on new Chinese optical transceivers that exists only as a draft rule. Nothing has been published in the Federal Register, so scope, timing and exemptions cannot be verified. Treat it as an option, not a catalyst.

author: semi-expert
text: Semiconductor expert: Supply constraint is management's own stated base case: Huang said NVIDIA expects to be constrained throughout the entire life of Vera Rubin, with Rubin beginning to contribute revenue in the following quarter. Upstream bottleneck theses therefore rest on the customer's own guidance.

author: fundamental
text: Fundamental analyst: Concentration is extreme in both directions: data centre was $75.2B of $81.6B total revenue, roughly 92%, and that segment sells to a handful of hyperscalers. A single capex deferral by one customer moves the whole company, which no supply-chain read-through captures.

author: pm
text: Portfolio manager: NVIDIA has de-rated relative to its own suppliers over the past year, so the asymmetry has moved downstream into the component names. Owning NVIDIA now is the low-variance expression of the same thesis, not the high-return one.

author: semi-expert
text: Semiconductor expert: Alphabet discloses cloud backlog but no TPU volumes, no capacity in megawatts and no accelerator mix. Third-party TPU unit estimates therefore cannot be validated against any filed figure, and read-throughs to specific optics or memory suppliers are inference, not disclosure.

author: fundamental
text: Fundamental analyst: The backlog is the number that matters and it is filed: Google Cloud revenue rose 82% to $24.8B and backlog reached $514B, with just over half expected to convert to revenue within 24 months. That is a contracted, dated demand signal rather than a narrative one.

author: pm
text: Portfolio manager: Alphabet is the cheapest large-cap way to own contracted AI demand, but the cash cost is now visible in the capex line, and the market re-rates it downward on every raise. What changes the call is backlog conversion stalling below the stated 24-month pace.

author: semi-expert
text: Semiconductor expert: The mix shift is real and disclosed: enterprise SSD demand drove the quarter and Sandisk began recognising revenue from its QLC-based Stargate platform. That is a datacenter NAND ramp, not a consumer cycle, which makes the pricing less likely to break on handset weakness.

author: fundamental
text: Fundamental analyst: The multiple is pricing a peak. Fiscal Q4 revenue was $8.97B with adjusted EPS of $39.25, and Q1 fiscal 2027 is guided to $10.3-$10.8B and $44-$46. Annualised, the share price is a single-digit multiple of guided earnings, which is what a cycle top looks like.

author: pm
text: Portfolio manager: The tape is trading the cycle, not the print: the stock beat, raised, and is still far below where it stood a month ago. In a commodity up-cycle the exit signal is contract price momentum rolling over, not an earnings miss, which arrives too late.

author: semi-expert
text: Semiconductor expert: POET is still pre-production. Q1 2026 revenue of $503,389 was non-recurring engineering, not product. The upgrade in wording from production-readiness to production with Sivers lasers by end-2026 is a company statement with no shipped volume behind it yet.

author: fundamental
text: Fundamental analyst: Dilution is the story the feed skips: shares outstanding rose about 74% in a year, including a 20.7m-share January placement. Working capital of $418.8M against roughly $8.8M quarterly operating cash burn funds years of runway, but existing holders paid for it.

author: pm
text: Portfolio manager: No financing risk and no revenue either. Cash covers many years of burn, so this is a long-dated option on the interposer qualifying, priced at over a billion dollars of market value on about two million dollars of annualised revenue. Size it like an option.

author: semi-expert
text: Semiconductor expert: The advanced-packaging squeeze is easing, not tightening. Industry data has the CoWoS supply-demand gap narrowing from about 20% to 10% by end-2026 as capacity expands toward roughly 200k wafers per month by end-2027. Bottleneck theses should migrate upstream to optics and substrates.

author: fundamental
text: Fundamental analyst: First-half 2026 revenue was NT$2,404bn, up 35.6% year over year, with June alone up 67.9%. Monthly disclosure makes TSMC the only name in this book where the demand curve can be checked every thirty days rather than every quarter.

author: pm
text: Portfolio manager: TSMC is the low-variance way to own the same buildout the book expresses through single-digit-billion suppliers trading at ten times sales. It gives up the upside and removes the qualification, dilution and single-customer risk carried by most of the watchlist.

author: aleabitoreddit
text:
Just putting it out there for people that think AAOI is a one year cycle...

$AAOI projects their ELSFP capacity for CPO to be 400K/units a month in 2028.

400k * ~$400 ELS ASP (GS assumptions) = + another ~$1.92B 2028 annualized revenue capacity added as a new distinct (>50% gross margin) product line. 

On top of their existing 2027 projections (eg. ~$5.6B annualized transceiver revenue off $471m/month entering H2).

author: aleabitoreddit
text:
Okay here's my take on $POET, since apparently people are celebrating on the subreddit that I took small positions. 

- I have 0 idea. ZERO. How they convinced shareholders to allow them dilute SO MUCH to the point:

They have an absurd ~$830m cash on hand now. 

And my guess is that they're close to done, since I would be in disbelief if they needed more. 

So now... they have ~$830m to grow their business like M&A, and EV actually dropped really low recently (eg. $1.25B MC vs. $830m cash on hand), that I thought it was compelling to take a risk. 

- Annualized production capacity target is 12M optical engines/year for 2027, which is pretty absurd ramp. 

Need to do more research into ASP for Poet's products, but maybe $125-$200? So at ~$150 ASP, $1.8B revenue ceiling. 

But they're like inverse AAOI right now: no visible demand to fill all that capacity. Aside from Lumilens, which is now a highly valued hyperscaler supplier (probably Amazon or Microsoft), with billions in customer agreements. 

The interesting thing is if Poet signed prepayment EML agreements with players like Mitsubishi, or CW agreements with Sivers behind the scenes with that balance sheet. 

And given the current bottleneck, players might use Poet as a workaround for supply procurement. 

But basically, you have a super cash-rich company with a ton of capacity coming online. And they're not really disappearing anytime soon with their financials. 

I don't quite think it's as technically defensible compared to upstream laser chokepoints with something like $SIVE around the same valuation in terms of technical moat for CW lasers vs. OE packaging side. As you've seen recently with Celestial and Poet. 

But maybe... there's a chance some hyperscaler or downstream company announces a volume agreement sometime in the future. and $POET takes off. And they do have the supply chain setup for ramp with that.

author: semi-expert
text: Semiconductor expert: Lumentum crossed 50% non-GAAP gross margin a full quarter ahead of its own timeline while shipping record 800G volume and starting 1.6T module production. Its internal laser capacity is scaling faster than planned, which makes the shortage a merchant-supply problem, not an industry yield problem.

author: fundamental
text: Fundamental analyst: FQ4 revenue $1.01B, up 109% year over year, at 36.6% non-GAAP operating margin. FQ1 FY27 is guided to $1.225-1.275B with non-GAAP EPS of $4.05-4.35 against $3.23 just delivered. The growth is in guidance, not in backlog commentary.

author: pm
text: Portfolio manager: At a guided $5B annualised run-rate and 40% operating margin, Lumentum is priced as a finished AI winner rather than the 2025 turnaround the desk bought. The asymmetry is gone. Downside is now a single hyperscaler order-timing slip against a very high bar.

author: semi-expert
text: Semiconductor expert: The SemiNex programme the analyst cites is a $3.4M development contract targeting early production in H2 2027. That is a qualification milestone, not capacity, and it changes no shipped volume in 2026 or 2027. No primary source located to confirm the contract terms.

author: fundamental
text: Fundamental analyst: Sivers' share price ran from SEK 10.71 to SEK 63.15 during Q2 while Q1 revenue fell 22% year over year to SEK 61.9M, and the company disclosed that revenue expected in H1 slips into H2. Q2 also carries a SEK 42.9M non-cash social-security charge.

author: pm
text: Portfolio manager: Sivers does not report Q2 until 27 August, after a roughly six-fold share move, and has already pre-announced revenue slippage. The desk holds a sticky accumulate into a print it has no numbers for. This is a position-sizing decision, not a conviction one.

author: semi-expert
text: Semiconductor expert: Management guided more than $70M of 1.6T revenue in Q4, which would be its first material 1.6T quarter. That is a ramp beginning, not a ramp proven, and customer qualification at that node remains a quarterly event risk.

author: fundamental
text: Fundamental analyst: The reiterated roughly $1.1B FY26 target needs Q4 revenue near $485M against a Q3 guide midpoint of $272M, a 78% sequential step in one quarter, off $343M of first-half revenue. The entire year rests on a quarter that has to nearly double.

author: pm
text: Portfolio manager: Q2 non-GAAP EPS was $0.06 on $191.9M of revenue, so profitability is one cent thick, and Q3 gross margin is guided to 29-30.5%, roughly twenty points below Lumentum's. A revenue miss here has no earnings cushion under it.

author: semi-expert
text: Semiconductor expert: MACOM's indium phosphide supply is secured through long-term epiwafer agreements and an equity stake in IQE, so it is less exposed to the merchant laser shortage than pure transceiver assemblers. No primary filing located confirming the stake size or agreement terms.

author: fundamental
text: Fundamental analyst: FQ3 revenue $342.2M, up 35.8% year over year, with FQ4 guided to $415-425M, another 21-24% sequential step, on a record 1.6 book-to-bill. Adjusted gross margin is guided to 60-61%, roughly double AAOI's.

author: pm
text: Portfolio manager: FQ4 guidance annualises to roughly $1.7B, so the multiple already assumes the datacenter step-up continues. MACOM enters the top fifteen on eleven mentions with no bear case in the feed and no desk verdict ever written. Size it as an initiation, not a conviction.

author: semi-expert
text: Semiconductor expert: Guiding Q2 GAAP gross margin at 74.9% means NVIDIA expects to absorb the HBM and advanced-packaging cost inflation its own suppliers are reporting without passing it through. That margin line, not the revenue line, is the supply-chain signal on 26 August.

author: fundamental
text: Fundamental analyst: NVIDIA has not reported since Q1 FY27: revenue $81.6B up 85%, data center $75.2B up 92%, GAAP gross margin 74.9%. Q2 FY27 is guided to $91.0B plus or minus 2% and lands 26 August. Every verdict this week is written ahead of that print.

author: pm
text: Portfolio manager: A $91B guide two quarters after $81.6B leaves no room for a supply-driven shortfall to be read as anything other than demand weakness. Holding into 26 August is a bet on the guide holding, which is a different risk from the buildout thesis.

author: semi-expert
text: Semiconductor expert: AMD launched the Instinct MI400 series including MI455X and MI430X in the quarter, so there is now a second rack-scale accelerator family in the market. HBM, substrate and optics pull-through becomes a two-vendor problem rather than a single-vendor one.

author: fundamental
text: Fundamental analyst: Q2 revenue was a record $11.5B, up 50% year over year, with data center $6.7B, up 107%, and 58% of company revenue. Q3 is guided to roughly $13B at about 56% gross margin, with data-center AI guided to well over 100% growth.

author: pm
text: Portfolio manager: AMD guides about 56% gross margin against NVIDIA's 74.9%: it is winning volume at structurally worse economics. The bet is share, not margin, and a $13B Q3 leaves little tolerance for an MI400 ramp slipping a quarter.

author: semi-expert
text: Semiconductor expert: Coherent doubled six-inch indium phosphide capacity ahead of plan and took datacenter and communications to 79% of Q4 revenue, up 59% year over year. Keeping InP lasers in-house is therefore an allocation choice, which makes merchant laser supply scarcer exactly as the analyst argues.

author: fundamental
text: Fundamental analyst: Record FQ4 revenue $2.05B, up 34% year over year; FY26 revenue $7.12B, up 22.5%, with non-GAAP EPS up 59% to $5.61. FQ1 FY27 is guided to $2.2-2.4B and non-GAAP EPS of $1.85-2.05.

author: pm
text: Portfolio manager: Coherent beat on every line and the stock fell, the same reaction Cisco and Applied Materials drew this week. Non-GAAP gross margin is guided to 39.5-41.5%, about ten points below Lumentum's. The market is repricing this group on margin, not on growth.

author: semi-expert
text: Semiconductor expert: Alphabet serves much of its cloud growth on internal TPUs, so each capex dollar converts into less merchant GPU, HBM and optics demand than a neocloud's does. Treat its headline capex as a weaker read-through to the desk's chain. No primary source quantifies the TPU share.

author: fundamental
text: Fundamental analyst: Q2 revenue $119.8B, up 24%, with Google Cloud $24.8B, up 82%, led by enterprise AI infrastructure and solutions. Consolidated operating margin still expanded two points to 34% while capital spending was scaling hard.

author: pm
text: Portfolio manager: Alphabet guided 2026 capital expenditure to $180-190B and said 2027 would increase significantly, then raised again at Q2. This is now a capex story as much as a search story, and the repricing risk sits in depreciation, not revenue.

author: semi-expert
text: Semiconductor expert: TrendForce has server DRAM contract prices rising 13-18% quarter over quarter in 3Q26 with long-term agreements capping the increase, and HBM contract prices multiples higher in 2027 against RDIMM bit supply growing only 15-20%. Supply sets the price, not demand.

author: fundamental
text: Fundamental analyst: FQ3 revenue was $41.46B against $23.86B the prior quarter and $9.30B a year earlier, with GAAP net income $28.24B. Data center revenue exceeded $25B, an annualised run-rate above $100B, and FQ4 was guided near $50B.

author: pm
text: Portfolio manager: Memory is now the highest-earning and most cyclical link in the chain. The exit signal is not a demand miss but the first quarter long-term-agreement pricing stops rising. Nothing in the 3Q26 contract data says that is close.

author: semi-expert
text: Semiconductor expert: Digit is deployed with Schaeffler, GXO, Toyota Motor Manufacturing Canada and Mercado Libre. Those are real deployments but disclosed as programmes, not volumes, so the per-robot compute, memory and lidar content driving the desk's read-through remains unquantified.

author: fundamental
text: Fundamental analyst: CCXI is a pre-close SPAC, not an operating company. The Agility Robotics combination was announced 24 June 2026 at about $2.5B, the Form S-4 was only confidentially submitted on 14 July, and closing still requires shareholder approval, SEC review and exchange listing.

author: pm
text: Portfolio manager: Agility's order book is not investable through CCXI until the S-4 clears and redemption levels are known, and the ticker becomes AGLT on close. A ninth-ranked Core position sitting in a trust vehicle is a structural risk the priority score cannot see.

author: semi-expert
text: Semiconductor expert: AWS capacity at this growth rate is gated by power and datacenter shell availability rather than silicon, which makes the desk's power layer a tighter read on AWS's 2027 ceiling than its accelerator layer. No primary source located that quantifies the constraint.

author: fundamental
text: Fundamental analyst: Q2 net sales $200.6B, up 20%, with AWS up 37%, its fastest growth in eighteen quarters, at a $169B annualised run-rate and $16.6B of segment operating income. Property and equipment purchases rose $66.1B year over year on AI.

author: pm
text: Portfolio manager: Trailing-twelve-month free cash flow swung to a $7.6B outflow on that spending. Amazon is funding the AI build from its balance sheet, so the equity risk has moved from growth to whether the depreciation is ever earned back.

author: semi-expert
text: Semiconductor expert: Monthly revenue is a shipment number, not a capacity number. It confirms advanced-node output is being consumed but says nothing about how CoWoS allocation splits between NVIDIA and AMD, which is where the 2027 constraint actually sits.

author: fundamental
text: Fundamental analyst: July net revenue was NT$467.58B, up 44.7% year over year and 5.6% month over month, with January through July at NT$2,872.06B, up 37.0%. Monthly disclosure removes any argument that the AI order book is still a forecast.

author: pm
text: Portfolio manager: TSMC is the lowest-variance way to own this buildout and the desk has never reflected that in its stance. At 37% year-to-date revenue growth the case against it is price and Taiwan concentration, not the business.

author: aleabitoreddit
text:
Since people are having fun speculating on $SKHY CPO roadmap supply chains.

I'm gonna do my own guess and say SK Hynix is evaluating Celestial/Ayar. Then doing heavy evaluation into microLEDs past first-gen deployments. 

Both have been kinda working on it for awhile. 

- Ayar shown up in SK hynix's own website in the context of optical <-> memory links. 
- Marvell is actively working with SK Hynix in custom memory solutions (and guess who owns Celestial now). 

Celestial/Ayar are both also cited in SK Hynix's linked Nature Paper, which helps a bit with technical relevance: 

(121): Stojanovic, V. A UCIe optical I/O retimer chiplet for AI scale-up. In 2025 IEEE Hot Chips 37 Symposium (HCS) 1–22 (IEEE, 2025) 

- This is Ayar reference (Ayar’s teraphy optical I/O chiplet), Stojanovic is Ayar Lab's co-founder btw. 

(123): Winterbottom, P. Photonic interconnect for accelerated computing celestial AI photonic fabric module (cough cough Celestial)

There's more breadcrumbs out there, but wanted to keep this relatively short-form. 

For more upstream beneficaries: 

-> I still think $SIVE is the cleanest read through since they're likely supplying to both Celestial/Ayar. 

The interposer/packaging IP layer... People were speculating $POET, but Marvell probably vertically integrated players them out this year after the announcement. 

Given they've had their own SiPH interposer tech/integration IP before Celestials acquisition (eg. presented a silicon-photonics interposer back in 2023)

-> AMS Osram (which I don't own), seems like they're co-developing in this area given they randomly went out of their way this year to say HBM <-> optics was a TAM increase for them. 

TLDR: I see Ayar/Celestial as candidates for SK Hynix's CPO roadmap, then microLEDs being commercialized past gen-1 maybe 2029. (this is all speculation)

Just to throw a bone to quantum dot bros, this got cited like 5 times. https://x.com/aleabitoreddit/status/2090735668532224224

views.why: Calls it the cleanest read-through on the SK Hynix CPO roadmap because it likely supplies both Celestial and Ayar, the two names he thinks are being evaluated

author: semi-expert
text: Semiconductor expert: Lumentum's Q4 release claims an initial ELS module order, rising ultra-high-power CPO laser demand and NPO engagements, but states no H2 2027 CPO shipment date. That timeline is call commentary, not a figure the filed release carries.

author: fundamental
text: Fundamental analyst: Shares outstanding went 69.9m to 89.7m, up 28% in twelve months, as convertibles were equitized. That produced a one-time $7.8bn non-cash extinguishment loss and a $7.2bn GAAP quarterly net loss. The analyst reported only non-GAAP per-share figures.

author: pm
text: Portfolio manager: At $841 Lumentum is roughly 25x FY2026 revenue of $3.01bn and 97x FY2026 non-GAAP EPS of $8.67. Annualising the Q1 FY2027 guide midpoint still leaves about 50x forward. The demand is real; the price assumes flawless execution through FY2028.

author: semi-expert
text: Semiconductor expert: Could not verify from a primary source the earnings-call quote that Coherent will not sell indium phosphide lasers externally. The Q4 release says only that capital allocation prioritises expanding manufacturing capacity. Treat the merchant-supply exclusion as unconfirmed.

author: fundamental
text: Fundamental analyst: Coherent's FY2026 non-GAAP gross margin was 39.4% and operating margin 20.5%, against Lumentum's 46.0% and 29.8%. But Coherent trades near 7.7x FY2026 revenue of $7.12bn versus roughly 25x for Lumentum. Weaker margins, materially cheaper entry to the same demand.

author: pm
text: Portfolio manager: Coherent's FY2026 GAAP operating margin was 12.6% against 20.5% non-GAAP, a 790bp gap from stock compensation and amortisation. Q4 revenue grew 33.8% year over year versus Lumentum's 109.3%. Owning Coherent is a bet on catch-up, not on the same growth rate.

author: semi-expert
text: Semiconductor expert: TrendForce forecasts 3Q26 NAND contract prices up only 10-15% quarter on quarter, a noticeably slower pace than previous quarters, citing weaker consumer demand and a higher base. Supply stays tight, but the rate of price increase has already turned down.

author: fundamental
text: Fundamental analyst: SanDisk's FY2026 GAAP gross margin was already 71.5%, $14.47bn on $20.25bn revenue, against 30.1% in FY2025 and 16.1% in FY2024. The 80% target is a small step from a shortage-set base, not a structural cost gain. That 55-point swing took one year.

author: pm
text: Portfolio manager: Minimum contracted revenue of $93bn sits against a market capitalisation near $221bn, so 2.4x the contracted book is already paid, and contracted revenue is not profit. At the guided 50% free cash flow margin that book is roughly $46bn of undiscounted cash.

author: semi-expert
text: Semiconductor expert: No Form S-4 is publicly filed for the Agility merger; the registration statement was submitted confidentially. There are therefore no audited Agility financials, no segment detail and no customer disclosure on file. The technical claims cannot be diligenced from primary sources.

author: fundamental
text: Fundamental analyst: The Exchange Ratio is Agility's per-share equity value divided by the trust redemption price, $10.17 at 30 June 2026, not by CCXI's market price. Buying at $14.16 pays about 1.39x that, an effective pre-money valuation near $3.5bn rather than the $2.5bn headline.

author: pm
text: Portfolio manager: Structure the headline hides: 13.8m founder Class B shares against 41.4m public shares, a $15.99m deferred underwriting fee payable only on closing, and a $201m PIPE priced at $10.00 while the open market pays $14.16. The deadline to close is 18 March 2028.

author: semi-expert
text: Semiconductor expert: Could not verify from a primary source that Applied Optoelectronics holds 300-400mW CW lasers, or that it is sold out through H2 2027. Both are conference remarks and appear in neither the 10-Q nor the August prospectus supplement.

author: fundamental
text: Fundamental analyst: Shares went 62.4m to 84.6m in twelve months, up 36%, and the new $600m ATM at $129.10 adds 4.65m more. That is the third raise since April, roughly $1.7bn, while first-half 2026 operating cash flow was negative $73.8m on $343m of revenue.

author: pm
text: Portfolio manager: The prospectus commits proceeds to general corporate purposes, which may include debt repayment, working capital, capital expenditures and acquisitions. Nothing earmarks the $600m for laser capacity. The capacity story is management's; the filing commits to none of it.

author: semi-expert
text: Semiconductor expert: The Portsmouth leases cover about 4.25GW of IT load with ready-for-service conditions expected beginning in 2028, plus optional credit support for 3.8GW more. The compute this secures is a 2028-and-beyond event, not a fiscal 2027 revenue contributor.

author: fundamental
text: Fundamental analyst: NVIDIA signed residual value guaranties on about 4.25GW of leases with aggregate payment obligation capped at $105bn, disclosed under Item 2.03 as an off-balance-sheet obligation. OpenAI is the tenant; on OpenAI insolvency or non-payment NVIDIA pays the shortfall.

author: pm
text: Portfolio manager: The guaranty agreements will be filed with the 10-Q for the quarter ended 26 July 2026, reported 26 August. That exhibit, not the revenue beat, is the thing to read: it sizes how much of its own demand NVIDIA is now underwriting.

author: semi-expert
text: Semiconductor expert: Sivers' Q1 report lists demonstrations of DFB laser arrays at OFC 2026 and partnerships with O-Net and Enablence. Those are engagements and demos, not qualified volume production. No filed document shows a production-volume laser design win at a named customer.

author: fundamental
text: Fundamental analyst: Q1 2026 net sales were SEK 61.9m, down 22% year over year, with EBITDA of negative SEK 24.7m. Against a market capitalisation near SEK 10.7bn that is roughly 43x annualised sales, on revenue that shrank. The laser revenue is not in the numbers yet.

author: pm
text: Portfolio manager: The $799m the bull case cites is an opportunity pipeline, up 77% year to date, not order backlog and not revenue. Management pushed defence revenue into the second half of 2026. The Q2 report on 27 August is the first test of that promise.

author: semi-expert
text: Semiconductor expert: Riot's own disclosure puts AMD at 50MW firmly contracted at Rockdale, 25MW delivered and 25MW targeted for November 2026 and May 2027. The $9.1bn, 191MW twenty-year lease grouped with it belongs to a different tenant, a frontier AI lab.

author: fundamental
text: Fundamental analyst: Q2 2026 revenue was $11.54bn, up 50% year over year, with gross profit $6.20bn, a 53.8% gross margin against 39.8% a year earlier. The margin expansion, not only the volume, is what the data-centre mix shift is delivering.

author: pm
text: Portfolio manager: At $458 AMD is roughly 16x annualised revenue after a 160% twelve-month run, so a 9% one-month drawdown is noise against the re-rating. Its Riot footprint is 50MW; the position rests on accelerator share, not on colocation capacity.

author: semi-expert
text: Semiconductor expert: Could not verify from a primary source the Marvell warrant terms or the $120bn-through-2033 revenue figure attributed to the TPU relationship. Neither appears in an Alphabet or Marvell filing I could read. Treat both as press characterisation.

author: fundamental
text: Fundamental analyst: Alphabet's Q2 2026 operating cash flow was $39.07bn against $44.92bn of capital expenditure, so free cash flow was negative $5.86bn, and 2026 capex guidance rose to $195-205bn. The bull case cites record cloud demand; the cash statement shows what serving it costs.

author: pm
text: Portfolio manager: First-half 2026 capex of $80.6bn already nearly matches full-year 2025's $91.4bn, and the cash cushion is gone. Alphabet's AI position is now funded from the balance sheet, so the multiple has to survive a capex cycle it cannot pause.

text: Semiconductor expert: Could not verify from a primary filing the claim that leading AI labs made multi-year, multi-gigawatt Trainium commitments, or the $25bn custom-silicon run rate. Both are earnings-call remarks and appear in no Amazon filing I could read.

author: fundamental
text: Fundamental analyst: Amazon's Q2 2026 operating cash flow was $45.39bn against $54.21bn of capital expenditure, so free cash flow was negative $8.82bn, and negative $26.99bn across the first half. Capex guidance rose to about $220bn on higher memory costs.

author: pm
text: Portfolio manager: First-half 2026 capex of $98.4bn is up 72% on $57.2bn a year earlier, and Amazon guides that capacity constraints persist into 2027. For this desk Amazon reads as a leading indicator for memory and optics, not as a position competing with them.

author: semi-expert
text: Semiconductor expert: MACOM guides fiscal Q4 revenue of $415-425m against $342.2m delivered, with adjusted gross margin rising to 60-61% from 59.7%. Capacity is converting into shipments and price at once, which is what a genuine bottleneck looks like from the supplier's side.

author: fundamental
text: Fundamental analyst: Q3 revenue was $342.2m, up 35.8% year over year, GAAP gross margin 58.3%, adjusted operating margin 31.5%. The Q4 guide implies about $8 of annualised adjusted EPS on 78.9m diluted shares, roughly 32x at $259, against Lumentum's 50x for the same demand.

author: pm
text: Portfolio manager: MACOM fell 15.6% in a week while guiding revenue up 21-24% sequentially and gross margin up 100bp. Nothing in the release explains the move, so the drawdown is positioning rather than a change in the filed numbers.

author: semi-expert
text: Semiconductor expert: TrendForce has conventional DRAM contract prices up 13-18% quarter on quarter in 3Q26 and NAND up 10-15%, but says weaker consumer demand and a higher comparison base will moderate the increases. The shortage holds; the second derivative of pricing has rolled over.

author: fundamental
text: Fundamental analyst: Micron's quarterly gross margin ran 56.0%, then 74.4%, then 84.6% across the three quarters to 28 May 2026, on revenue rising $13.6bn to $41.5bn. That 84.6% is above the 80% SanDisk targets for 2030. No memory cycle has held a peak near this.

author: pm
text: Portfolio manager: At $919 Micron carries a $1.04trn market capitalisation on roughly $166bn of annualised revenue and $140bn of annualised gross profit. That is fair only if 84.6% gross margin is a plateau, not a peak. Size the position off the margin, not the shortage.

author: aleabitoreddit
text:
Thoughts on this 1.9x P/E memory company: (annualized off recent ER)

Spent a lot of time going through the memory stack for new 
$SNDK
 style names because cascading structural shortages from HBM/DDR5 into DDR4/DDR3/DDR2.  

ESMT at $2.5B MC caught my interest.

Here's a note from my high-level thoughts/research on this name:

July's (1 month) earnings were:
- $212.8M revenue / $109.5M (net income, +- few M depending on FX)

Annualized that's: $1.314B net income/year off a $2.5B MC, so 1.9x July runrate P/E.

- Cash on hand: $455.7M (~$395.9M net cash)
- $943.5M assets
- $249.6M inventory, $146.3M receivables
- $596.0M book equity

They ~$359.6M net income in the first seven months of 2026, and it's accelerated to ~$109.5M a month net income. 

What's even more interesting is Winbond is gradually withdrawing from DDR2 (June Trendforce report), which should give increased leverage to ESMT H2 (with price forecasts of DDR2 being 35-40% Q3)

What's not disclosed is wafer allocations from PSMC and possible risk is margin decrease due to upstream wafer hikes. 

(You can think of an analogy like Kioxia: PSMC, ESMT: Sandisk, but without ownership)

PSMC did raise DRAM wafer-start prices about 45% (started in July, maybe shows up Nov/Dec) and ESMT said H2 margins could slip due to wafers having a higher cost.

So wanted to look at the bear case, and do some speculative napkin math wafer calculations based on their "2026 wafer capacity is roughly unchanged from 2025 and only satisfies ~60–70% of customer demand" claims

Napkin math: 

ESMT did ~NT$13.5B revenue in 2024 at near 0 profitability, so monthly COGS was ~$30M, of which wafers might be $20M. 

A 45% hike on that base gets you somewhere around ~$9M/month headwind. 

For a harsher stress test, using Q2's ~31.3% COGS/revenue ratio as a proxy for July, July's $212.8M rev would imply roughly $66.6M of monthly COGS.

If  100% of that were exposed to the +45% DRAM wafer repricing: would imply roughly a $30M/month pretax headwind

-> net income would fall to $85M/month, or about 2.45× annualized P/E (which is still pretty impressive)

Fun thing is July's net income report was only because TWSE forced a supplemental disclosure after abnormal trading. 

So, with Winbond winding down their segments, and DRAM est. going up Q/Q, signals point to ESMT maintaining similar profitability levels. There's DDR3 and others as main exposure, but DDR4 hikes trickles down the stack. 

Revenue growth looks like:

Feb 2026: $65.6M
March: $95.1M
April: $145.3M
May: $140.3M
June: $152.2M
July: $212.8M

Jan–July as a whole:
~$879M revenue
~$360M net income

But the issue most of the times is durability:

There's going to be folks saying "oh it's just July, look at TTM" but each quarter legacy DRAM keeps getting hiked, and there's further hikes ahead (so TTM is the wrong way to go), but maybe $100m+ net income a month is an anomaly, we'll see what other earnings are. 

Out of the Teamgroup/Apacer/ADATA/Innodisk/Etron type names I looked at that actually can maintain pricing power as well (and not just flipping inventory).

Felt like ESMT was the winner of the bunch (where cash just keeps flowing into balance sheet) given wafer allocations and an substantial increase in gross profit.

And durable are earnings + the shortage?

- “DDR4 / LPDDR4 structural supply gap remains evident through 2028 and onward" Winbond's May 2026 investor presentation (which supports further cascading)

Winbond had characterized DDR4/DDR3 as having ongoing structural supply gaps with "no near-term resolution"

- TrendForce says OEMs unable or unwilling to secure DDR4 are redesigning/down-specing into DDR3, which then forces DDR3 users toward DDR2

- There's not much coverage or players in DDR2 despite its importance now... which is appreciated.  

TLDR:

views.why: Named only as the style of setup he was hunting for when he found ESMT; the analysis is entirely about ESMT

author: aleabitoreddit
text:
I actually allocated a sizeable amount to the legacy DRAM trade (did legacy NAND/NOR Q1 this year). 

And made legacy DRAM a medium term trade. Since I'm starting to see substantial price hikes and demand imbalance statements.   

Just some of my personal notes on July runrates: 

ESMT (3006) - $2.53B MC, 1.94x P/E
Etron (5351) - $1.19B, 4.15x P/E
Winbond (2344) - $25.3B, ~6.2x P/E
Nanya (2408) - $55.3B, ~5.5x P/E
PSMC (6770) - $9.4B, ~19.6x P/E
TeamGroup (4967) - $728M, ~2.4x P/E
Transcend (2451) - $4.06B, ~3.3x P/E
Innodisk (5289) - $4.57B, ~3.1x P/E
Apacer (8271) - $937M, ~3.2x P/E
ADATA (3260) - $4.40B, ~2.3x PE
Silicon Power (4973), $318M, ~4.1x P/E

- ESMT (fabless) extraordinary net income growth, wafer supplier in Taiwan, pass through cost, DDR2/DDR3 structurally undersupplied, I see earnings durability throughout 2027, which is why 1.94X P/E was extmreley interesting

- Etron (fabless) I covered before, but monthly profitability is exploding over time, they have a JV with Nanya which kicks off in 2027, and probably my second favorite name

- Winbond, is probably my favorites up there since they actually own fabs and captures downstream products, rather than just wafers like PSMC. Demand visibility I think extends to 2029-2030 now form initial discussions, not exacty an undiscovered name anymore, but I do think it gets re-rated given price hikes/low forward p/e. Maybe 3.5x 2027 earnings for Winbond.. which is also really stellar, but 1.9x current 2026 earnings from ESMT was just insane.

Would say something similar to Nanya that owns DRAM fabs, but Nayna is already well covered.

- Teamgroup expected worse memory shortage around H1 2027, tightening beyond 2027, and they have massive inventory. But it's very inventory heavy type profit. 

- TeamGroup, ADATA (extremely inventory heavy), Apacer, Innodisk and Silicon Power had rapidly growing inventory but failed my own cash conversion test (so I placed them in the inventory beneficiaries). 

I'm sure I might have missed some nuance here, but for the sake of time/modeling, wanted a 
$SNDK
 style name that was actively converting into profitability. 

Since a lot of them just stocked up or profited off on inventory (which also should translate to earnings) but... despite their low P/E actually lost money H1 or with Transcend issued convertible bonds/dilution to fund it. 

- Transcend is probably the one I'm going to look at a bit further, just did lite DD so far since gross margin hit 77%. 

- PSMC fwd p/e is a bit higher compared to the rest but they're hiking wafer costs ~45%, so maybe you get ~6.7–9.5× forward P/E, buttt maybe they keep hiking.

TLDR:

-> Liked Etron, ESMT since there's a lot of earnings discovery recently, and would get priced in sooner or later. 
-> Nanya/Winbond are probably the most durable of them all. 

I do think DDR2/DDR3 trade is more uncharted terrtiory versus your HBM/NAND Samsung/Sk Hynix/Micron, etc.  

And we're starting to see another 
$SNDK
 type cycle (but maybe less durable, not sure).  

Just a notes/thoughts here.

views.why: Used as the archetype he was screening for — a name actively converting price hikes into profit — while the actual positions he argues are Taiwanese legacy DRAM names

text:
I wanted exposure to DDR2/DDR3 bottleneck ongoing and found ESMT (3006). 

A $2.5B MC fabless company with PSMC wafer allocation (esp. focused on DDR2). 

Last month's net income was: $109.5M (July month), which annualized is $1.31B net profit (1.9x runrate P/E). 

If we look at net profit throughout the months tracking legacy DRAM price hikes:

Jan 2026: ~$16M (est)
Feb 2026: ~$17M
Mar 2026: ~$31M (est)
April 2026: ~$58M
May 2026: ~$60M (est)
June 2026: ~$67M (est)
Jul 2026: ~$110M
(Estimated months are inferred from reported quarterly totals. July is company reported)

This earnings progression reminds me of $SNDK style price hikes + earnings inflection (esp. the report released this month). 

And I do expect DDR2/DDR3 capacity to remain constrained throughout 2027 (with legacy players like Winbond withdrawing from certain lines too like DDR2).

It's not quite all inventory liquidation like the other peers. Sure lower cost inventory helped, but the primary driver seems to be the widening spread between wafer costs/supply and legacy dram ASPs?

Their balance sheet is extremely solid as well:

- Cash on hand: ~$395.9M net cash
- $249.6M inventory, $146.3M receivables

And the net income progression... is before further legacy DRAM hikes expected in Q3. 

*disclosure own positions, NFA

It's always a bit daunting being early without much commentary around the idea. Wondering if anyone can stress test this thesis?

Since a company that grew monthly net income from $16M -> $100m this year alone (July Annualized would be 1.9x P/E). 

And benefits from another projected wave of DDR2/DDR3 hikes this quarter... maybe like 35-40% for DDR2 lines per Trendforce, and DDR3 likely continuing to rise. 

Do markets just not know about this bottleneck/company or am I missing something from my research? https://x.com/aleabitoreddit/status/2092789800428622128

author: aleabitoreddit
text:
$SIVE ER transcript just dropped, TLDR:

- 6 NEW pluggable players working with Sivers now.

Probably the biggest news of the entire ER next to new foundry allocations. 

"3 are in alpha sample evaluation stage" and another 3 in technical engagement / supply assessment stage."

And now it makes more sense why their $1.2B revenue pipeline ballooned (since this was a bigger leap than Jabil). 

- Initial production orders with $JBL expected in the first half of 2027, with the production ramp planned second half of 2027

LFG, Jabil is a massive hyperscaler supplier and finally got clear timelines on revenue from volume ramp.

- "new foundry partner who has brought on tremendous capacity that is available now"

This is what I wanted to hear. Apparently they've been in the works for this for awhile since it's "available now", and THIS IS VERY MATERIAL. 

CW lasers are in a massive shortage and $SIVE brought on new supply outside of Win Semi (also de-risks).

As you hear with other qualified CW players (anything they make gets sold), so as Sivers partners finishes their qualifications, I'm expecting the same.

- "long-term capacity model where one-third of manufacturing capacity will be internal, while two-thirds will come from our foundry partners"

Lukewarm on this, it makes sense they need to be vertically integrated like $AAOI / $LITE eventually but implies more capex (better after NASDAQ listing).

As you see with ESMT + DDR2 bottlenecks, the operating income they get from just securing wafers during shortages and doing fabless models is incredible. 

And it would make more sense to fund this with cashflow down the road.

- NASDAQ listing ongoing. CFO gave a very lawyer like answer, but on track as usual.

- "We do not see production capacity as a bottleneck at this point in time"

This is very meaningful since with their new foundry partners, implies $SIVE is coming online with a very material CW laser supply to a bottlenecked market.

TLDR:
- NEW substantial FOUNDRY ALLOCATION! (very, very material during CW laser shortage)
- 6 new pluggable players outside of $JBL 
- Clear revenue ramp timelines from Jabil

Heavy focus on pluggables -> NPO -> CPO seems like the progression.  Only lukewarm piece was building up internal capacity but it's long term positive.  

Anyway, very happy after reading the transcript aside from potential capex prioritizing laser capacity (which is fine too during an industry shortage) over IP acquisition.

The 6 new pluggable players + substantial wafer allocation "available now" is a pretty insane disclosure. https://x.com/aleabitoreddit/status/2093054882282651723
